newsitem.title: USA: Iowa governor touts balanced budget amendment.
newsitem.headline: Iowa governor touts balanced budget amendment.

text.p: Iowa's Republican Governor Terry Branstad said on Saturday President Clinton could not be trusted to balance the federal budget and urged Americans to press for a historic change in the Constitution that would make it a requirement.

In the Republican response to Clinton's radio address, Branstad said he knew a balanced budget amendment would work, pointing to the fact that 49 of the 50 states already had the requirement written into their constitutions.

"In state after state, budgets are balanced ... and despite what opponents say, fiscal discipline will be beneficial to the country just as it has benefited the states with more quality jobs and higher incomes," he said.

Clinton and others consider a balanced budget amendment unnecessary, and complain it could cause major problems in the future when economic, political and social conditions might be radically different.

The amendment would put into the Constitution the current concept of using Social Security trust funds to reduce the deficit. Last year's $107 billion budget deficit would have reached $171 billion without the Social Security surplus.
Opponents believe that mandating the use of Social Security funds to balance the budget could endanger the program and payments to senior citizens in the future.

The amendment has been in the works for 60 years and came close to passage in 1995 when it got through the House but lost in the Senate by one vote. The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the measure again Thursday and the full chamber was expected to vote later this month.
"President Clinton and those who oppose a balanced budget amendment claim that it is unnecessary --- that they will balance the budget anyway -- if we just trust them," Branstad said.
"Let me ask you: do you really have confidence that the president will balance the budget now after he vetoed the first balanced budget passsed by a Congress since the 1960s?"
Branstad, predicting the amendment had "a better chance than ever" of passage, urged Americans to ask their senators and representatives to vote for it.

"The balanced budget amendment will hold the president and the Congress accountable to the people. It will change the way the federal government does business ... by forcing our leaders to be fiscally responsible," he said.

If the proposed 28th Constitutional amendment clears Congress by the required two-thirds vote in each house, it will have seven years to win ratification by 38 of the 50 states. Though Clinton opposes it, he cannot veto a Constitutional amendment.
The president next week will unveil his fiscal 1998 budget, which covers the year beginning Oct. 1. His spending plan aims for balance by 2002.
